body:
What is miniature painting?

Miniature painting is a tradition of producing detailed paintings on relatively small, portable surfaces, particularly paper, palm leaves and cloth. Many early examples were illustrations in handwritten books called manuscripts. Others were independent paintings preserved in albums.

Because a miniature was usually viewed from close range, painters could include carefully drawn figures, clothing, ornaments, buildings, animals and plants. Its small size did not mean that the subject was simple. A single painting could represent a historical event, an episode from literature or several related incidents.

Miniatures must be distinguished from murals, which are painted directly on walls or other architectural surfaces. They must also be distinguished from sculpture and from later large-format easel paintings. Size alone is not a sufficient identifying feature: some illustrated projects, especially the Mughal Hamzanama, used unusually large folios.

How illustrated manuscripts were organised

An individual manuscript leaf is called a folio. Text and painting could occupy separate portions of the same folio, or the text could appear on its reverse. Several folios illustrating a literary work formed a series. They were commonly stored together rather than permanently displayed on walls.

A manuscript's colophon, when preserved, may identify its patron, artist, scribe, place and date. This information is important because many surviving miniatures have become separated from their original manuscripts. When a dated colophon is missing, the date or place of a painting may be an attribution rather than a firmly established fact.

Painting was closely connected with patronage. Kings, nobles, religious institutions and prosperous merchants commissioned works and supported artists. Their interests influenced the subjects represented. Buddhist monasteries needed illustrated religious texts; Jain donors commissioned manuscripts for libraries; Mughal emperors supported historical chronicles and portraits; and regional rulers commissioned literary, devotional and court paintings.

What makes a painting school distinct?

A painting school is a recognised artistic tradition associated with a region, court or community. Its identity depends on a combination of features rather than a single colour or subject.

  • Patronage: Who commissioned and supported the painters?
  • Subject matter: Were the paintings religious manuscripts, literary illustrations, portraits, court records or studies of nature?
  • Visual features: Were figures strongly outlined or softly modelled? Were the colours brilliant or subdued? How were landscapes and faces represented?
  • Historical context: Which other painting traditions influenced the school?

The broad historical pattern

The Pala and Western Indian Jain traditions provide important early examples of illustrated manuscripts. From the 16th century, the Mughal, Rajasthani and Deccani courts developed distinctive traditions. Painting also flourished in the western Himalayan hill states, where the Pahari tradition developed from the late 17th century onward.

These schools did not simply replace one another. Their periods overlapped, and artists, paintings, manuscripts and artistic ideas travelled between courts.

A miniature painting's subject does not automatically identify its school. A Krishna painting may belong to a Rajasthani, Pahari, Mughal or Deccani tradition. The patron, place, date and visual treatment must also be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Miniatures are generally portable paintings, often associated with illustrated manuscripts and albums.
  • A folio is a manuscript leaf; a colophon may record the artist, patron, place and date.
  • Pala painting is associated with Buddhist manuscript production in eastern India.
  • Western Indian Jain manuscript painting has a particularly important connection with Gujarat.
  • Mughal, Rajasthani, Pahari and Deccani schools developed under different regional and royal patrons.
  • Trap: These traditions overlap in time and cannot be arranged as a single sequence in which one school completely replaced another.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 1, The Manuscript Painting Tradition, pp. 1-3; NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, p. 128, 2020-21 edition.]

title: Miniature Painting in India: Meaning, Development and Major Schools

body:
The Pala dynasty and the setting of the school

The Pala School of Painting developed in eastern India, particularly in the regions corresponding to present-day Bihar and Bengal. It is associated with the Pala dynasty, which ruled from approximately 750 CE to the middle of the 12th century.

The Pala period witnessed an important late phase of Buddhist art in India. Buddhist rulers and religious institutions supported monasteries, scholarship, manuscript preparation and image-making. Two major centres were Nalanda and Vikramashila, both located in the region of present-day Bihar.

These monasteries were centres of Buddhist learning as well as artistic production. Illustrated manuscripts were prepared for religious instruction, study and preservation. The paintings frequently represented subjects associated with Vajrayana Buddhism.

Materials, subjects and visual features

Many surviving Pala illustrations were painted on palm leaves. Because a palm leaf is long and narrow, the painted image had to be arranged within a restricted horizontal space. Religious figures could appear alongside manuscript text, and painted wooden covers protected the leaves.

The principal features of Pala painting include:

  • Religious subject matter: Buddhist figures and subjects associated particularly with Vajrayana traditions.
  • Flowing lines: Curved, continuous outlines give figures a relatively graceful and rounded appearance.
  • Subdued colours: Colour treatment is generally softer than the sharply contrasting, brilliant palette found in many Western Indian Jain manuscripts.
  • Relationship with sculpture: Painted figures and contemporary Pala sculptural images share important conventions of bodily form and ornament.

The contrast between Pala and Jain manuscript painting is especially useful. Pala painting is noted for flowing, sinuous lines, whereas Western Indian Jain painting commonly uses more angular, thin and emphatic outlines. These are identifying tendencies, not rules that apply equally to every surviving painting.

The Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita

One of the best-known illustrated texts associated with the Pala tradition is the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita, meaning the Perfection of Wisdom in 8,000 Lines. It is a Buddhist text, not a Jain scripture.

An important illustrated manuscript was prepared at Nalanda during the 15th regnal year of Pala king Ramapala, in the last quarter of the 11th century. The manuscript, now in the Bodleian Library at Oxford, has 6 illustrated pages and painted wooden covers.

A Pala-period illustration of Lokeshvara from an Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita manuscript, dated around 1050, is also reproduced in the NCERT textbook and identified with the National Museum, New Delhi.

Influence beyond eastern India

Students, pilgrims and monks travelled to centres such as Nalanda and Vikramashila. Manuscripts and Buddhist images circulated with them. Consequently, Pala artistic conventions influenced regions including Nepal, Tibet, Burma, Sri Lanka and Java.

The destruction and disruption of major Buddhist monasteries during the early 13th century contributed to the end of this tradition as a major centre of manuscript painting in eastern India. This does not mean that all Buddhist art or manuscript painting ended throughout Asia.

Prelims focus

  • Region: Eastern India, especially Bihar and Bengal.
  • Patronage: Pala rulers and Buddhist monastic institutions.
  • Centres: Nalanda and Vikramashila.
  • Religion: Buddhism, particularly Vajrayana subjects.
  • Text: Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita; an illustrated Nalanda manuscript is associated with Ramapala.
  • Trap: Pala painting is not the Gujarat-centred Jain manuscript tradition.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 1, Pala School of Painting, p. 9.]

body:
Why Gujarat became a major centre

The Western Indian School of Painting flourished particularly in Gujarat, with related activity in southern Rajasthan and western parts of central India. Its development was connected with prosperous trading communities, religious institutions and the patronage of local rulers and wealthy households.

Jain merchants and bankers were especially important patrons of illustrated manuscripts. The Jain religious tradition gave considerable importance to preserving, copying, donating and studying sacred texts. Within the broader Western Indian School, the paintings illustrating Jain subjects are commonly called the Jain School of Painting.

Patrons, libraries and manuscript donations

A distinctive form of patronage was shastradaan, the donation of religious books. Wealthy devotees commissioned manuscripts and donated them to monasteries and libraries known as bhandars. These repositories protected handwritten works and helped sustain the tradition of manuscript illustration.

The Chaulukya or Solanki rulers of medieval Gujarat supported Jain religious institutions. The 12th-century ruler Kumarapala is recorded as commissioning and distributing copies of the Kalpasutra and supporting the establishment of monastic libraries in Patan. Later inscriptions and manuscript records show the particularly important role of lay merchants and traders as donors.

It is important to distinguish these stages of patronage: Kumarapala belonged to the 12th century, whereas many surviving richly illustrated paper manuscripts are from later centuries. They must not all be treated as manuscripts personally commissioned by him.

Important Jain texts and their subjects

TextPrincipal subjectExam distinction
KalpasutraLives and important events associated with Jain Tirthankaras and religious teachersFrequently illustrated Jain manuscript
KalakacharyakathaAdventures of Acharya Kalaka, including the rescue of his sisterNarrative associated with Acharya Kalaka
Uttaradhyayana SutraTeachings and monastic conduct associated with MahaviraReligious instruction and conduct
Sangrahini SutraJain cosmological ideas and the structure of the universeCosmological illustrations

Kalpasutra illustrations include episodes from the life of Mahavira. A particularly recognisable subject in the Shvetambara tradition is the series of 14 auspicious dreams associated with his mother, Trishala. The Kalpasutra also has an important place in the annual Paryushana observances of Shvetambara Jains.

Materials and identifying features

The earliest surviving painted Jain palm-leaf manuscripts from western India date to approximately the 11th century. The illustrated Oghaniryukti manuscript dated 1060 is an early datable example preserved at Jaisalmer.

Initially, painters worked on narrow palm leaves and on the protective wooden covers called patlis. Paper became important from the 14th century, allowing larger painted sections and more elaborate compositions.

Characteristic features include:

  • Brilliant colours: Prominent reds, blues and yellows, with gold used lavishly in some later manuscripts.
  • Strong outlines: Thin, wiry and often angular lines around figures.
  • Stylised faces: Large eyes, frequently with a projecting far eye visible beyond the profile of the face.
  • Divided compositions: Text and illustrations arranged in separate spaces on a folio.
  • Decorative details: Carefully represented textiles, ornaments, furnishings and architectural features.

The projecting far eye in Western Indian Jain painting is a convention for depicting a face. It should not be confused with a religious or spiritual third eye.

Gujarat examples and their significance

Gujarat's manuscript heritage provides direct examples of this school. The NCERT textbook reproduces a Kalpasutra painting from Gujarat dated around 1475. It also identifies a Kalakacharyakatha manuscript dated 1497 and a 17th-century Sangrahini Sutra illustration in the N. C. Mehta Collection, Ahmedabad.

The location of a present-day collection is not automatically the place where a painting was produced. Ahmedabad is important here as a centre preserving examples of Indian manuscript and miniature painting, while the broader Western Indian tradition has a genuine historical connection with Gujarat.

Jain painting and the wider Western Indian tradition

Not all Western Indian manuscripts illustrate Jain texts. Paintings of literary works such as Chaurpanchashika and Gita Govinda belong to a wider indigenous tradition that developed alongside Jain manuscript painting. This tradition contributed visual features to later Rajasthani painting.

Consequently, Western Indian is a regional and artistic description, while Jain painting identifies an important religious and thematic branch within that wider tradition.

Prelims focus

  • Major region: Gujarat, with related centres in Rajasthan and western central India.
  • Principal patrons: Jain merchants, bankers, religious donors and some rulers.
  • Institutions: Bhandars were manuscript repositories; shastradaan means donation of books.
  • Important texts: Kalpasutra, Kalakacharyakatha, Uttaradhyayana Sutra and Sangrahini Sutra.
  • Visual clue: Bright colours, angular outlines and a projecting far eye.
  • Trap: Chaurpanchashika belongs to the wider indigenous painting tradition and is not itself a Jain canonical text.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Class 12, reprint 2025-26, Chapter 1, Western Indian School of Painting, pp. 3-8; John Guy, Jain Manuscript Painting, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, January 2012, sections on manuscript patronage and the development of the western Indian style, consulted 23 November 2026.]
